title: The 1-Bit Trick That Makes Giant Models Tiny #ai #tech #shorts
description:
PrismML Bonsai runs a 27B model on an iPhone — a 1-bit LLM from a Caltech spin-off that squeezes Qwen 3.6 from 54 GB down to 4 GB and runs local AI on-device, no cloud.

Everyone said a 27-billion-parameter model couldn't fit on a phone. PrismML did it with patented math, not normal compression. Bonsai stores each weight as a single sign bit — plus or minus one — bundling 128 of them under one shared float16 scale, so the math still runs in float16 but the memory footprint collapses. The claim: 14× less memory, 8× faster, 5× less energy, and over 10× the intelligence density of a standard model. And it's not iPhone-only — the open Bonsai demo runs on Mac, CUDA, Vulkan, ROCm, and plain CPU, with an 8B model at roughly 2.5 GB. You can test a 1-bit model on your own machine today.

top_reply.author: @TheStigma
top_reply.text:
It's not quantization - and that's the key distinction that changes everything. The model is natively trained from scratch for 1-bit weights. That precision cut does come with SOME penalties compared to 32/16bit - but it's already demonstrated that it works - and works surprisingly well. But training an LLM from scratch is seriously expensive, so that's why 8B is all that is available so far - and 8B just isn't competitive these days. Once this comes out in like a 70B model and you can still run that on your home hardware your mind will be blown.

The closest thing I can point you to for state-of-the-art local models is QAT (quantization aware training). I highly recommend you try out Gemma4 Q4_0 QAT. I'll be happy to recommend you one. it turns out that even the "hacky" solution of training the model a bit extra at the end to handle Q4 closer to natively is massively impactful. The result is that Q4 QAT is something like above 99% accuracy compared to the 16bit equivalent. It completely blows the most advanced quantization methods out of the water and makes them irrelevant (although, insanely enough, many of them could in theory stack as optimiztions, but thye need a lot of re-tooling of the methods). Just as you would expect - it makes a lot of the aggressive quantization "weirdness" you mention also largely disappear.  I highly recommend you try it. Unfortunately it's really only Gemma4 (ie Google) that has done this yet - but the research method is open for anyone to use. It doesn't need a full retraining, but it's still heavy enough that you need more than just enthusiast community members to do it on model sizes above 2-4B. We need to see some uptadted re-releases (which is exactly what they did for Gemma4). If we see this happpen for Qwen3.6 and others soon this will be another massive sea-change for local compute.

The point here being that QAT is a pale imitation hacky post-training fix compared to what can be done if the model is trained from scratch to be fully native at the lower precision level. It's just something you can benefit from massively right now.

Though honestly, 1bit isn't the future. Trinary (1.58bit) is. Thankfully they are developing that route at the same time, and Bonsai exists in trinary also. Not only is trinary a far more optimal balance point (likely THE optimal point mathematically) - but at trinary computing you can run the inference with stupidly simple addition math rather than matrix multiplications. Ironically this stuff will much faster on any modern CPU than on your GPU.

You can run and try both 1bit and trinary Bonsai 8B right now. They work just fine - and perform similarly to other 8B models in smarts at stupidly low memory footprints. Unfortunately you can only get the memory footprint benefits so far. All the (massive) compute benefits are mostly lost on current hardware because it has to be emulated to the lack of native support for these data-sizes. For trinary models to fully bloom to maximum potential we need to see some fundamental hardware reworking. Likely some native trinary acceleration chips. If you built a native trinary math chip it would be so stupidly efficient it would just be a small chiplet coprocessor on a CPU package.

So with all respect - don't make the mistake of discounting this as a concept. It's not hypothetical. It just need some big player investment to reach parity with the much more entrenched ecosystem.
